lesson.title: 381 Days: The Montgomery Bus Boycott
lesson.summary: After Rosa Parks's arrest in December 1955, Montgomery's Black community sustained a year long boycott of the city's segregated bus system, combining grassroots organizing, a young minister's leadership, and a federal court victory to win a major early civil rights victory.
lesson.body:
By 1955, Montgomery, Alabama's city buses required Black passengers to sit in a rear section and, if the front white section filled up, to give up their seats, and even entire rows, for white riders. Black riders made up the large majority of bus passengers in the city, which meant the system depended financially on the very people it treated as second class. Local activists, including Jo Ann Robinson of the Women's Political Council, had been quietly preparing for a bus boycott for some time, watching for the right moment and the right case to build one around.

That moment came on December 1, 1955, when Rosa Parks, secretary of the Montgomery chapter of the NAACP, was arrested for refusing to give up her seat to a white passenger. Within days, Robinson's network had distributed thousands of leaflets calling for a one day boycott of the buses on December 5, the date of Parks's trial. The boycott's overwhelming success that first day convinced organizers to continue it indefinitely, and local ministers and community leaders formed the Montgomery Improvement Association to coordinate the effort, electing a twenty six year old newcomer to town, the Reverend Martin Luther King Jr. of Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, as its president, in part because he was well respected but had not yet made local enemies.

Sustaining the boycott for over a year required serious organization. Since most Black residents did not own cars, the Montgomery Improvement Association organized an elaborate carpool system with hundreds of volunteer drivers and pickup points across the city, while others walked, sometimes for miles, rather than ride the segregated buses. Boycotters faced real retaliation, including arrests under an old anti boycott law and the bombing of King's own home, but the boycott held.

The boycott ended through a combination of economic pressure and a legal victory that built directly on the constitutional reasoning of Brown v. Board of Education the year before. Four Montgomery women, including Aurelia Browder and Claudette Colvin, who had been arrested for a similar refusal months before Parks, served as plaintiffs in a federal lawsuit, Browder v. Gayle, arguing that bus segregation violated the Fourteenth Amendment's guarantee of equal protection, the same constitutional ground Brown had relied on. A federal court agreed in June 1956, and the Supreme Court affirmed that ruling in November 1956. When the order finally reached Montgomery in December, the boycott ended after 381 days, having proven that a sustained, well organized mass protest could force real change, and having introduced Martin Luther King Jr. to the national stage as a civil rights leader.
